title: Seek Predicate vs Residual Predicate
description: An index covering only the leading column applies the rest as a residual predicate after a per-row lookup; put the filter columns in the key so they become seek predicates. Why it matters: a plan can show an Index Seek and STILL be doing far more work than necessary -- recognizing a residual predicate is what separates a real fix from a false sense of security.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
One of the more dangerous habits in query tuning is treating 'I see an Index Seek in the plan' as automatic proof that the query is efficient. Seeing a Seek instead of a Scan is genuinely good news most of the time — but this lesson exists precisely because it isn't a guarantee. A plan can show an Index Seek and *still* be doing dramatically more work than the actual result requires, and the reason lies in a distinction most people never learn to look for: the difference between a **seek predicate** and a **residual predicate**.

When SQL Server uses an index to seek, it needs to figure out exactly which part of your WHERE clause it can use to actually narrow down *where in the index* to start reading — that's the **seek predicate**. It can only use columns for this that are part of the index's key, evaluated in order from the leading column onward. Any *other* condition in your WHERE clause that isn't covered by the index's key gets applied afterward, row by row, on whatever rows the seek predicate already pulled up — that's called a **residual predicate** (sometimes just shown as a plain 'Predicate' in the plan, as opposed to 'Seek Predicate'). The crucial thing to understand is that a residual predicate is checked *after* the rows have already been fetched — it doesn't reduce how much work the seek itself has to do; it only filters the output *after* the expensive part is already done.

Here's the concrete version of that idea in this lesson: there's an index on `Orders(CustomerId)`, and the query filters on both `CustomerId = 42 AND Status = 'Open'`. Since the index's key only contains `CustomerId`, that's the *only* part of the WHERE clause the seek can actually use to narrow its starting point — the seek predicate is just `CustomerId = 42`. And customer 42, it turns out, has 4,000 orders total, only about 200 of which are currently `'Open'`. The index seek dutifully finds and retrieves all 4,000 of that customer's orders (because from the index's point of view, `CustomerId = 42` is exactly what it was asked to seek to, and it has no idea about `Status` at all). Then, and only then, does SQL Server check each of those 4,000 retrieved rows against the *remaining* condition, `Status = 'Open'`, discarding the roughly 3,800 that don't match and keeping the 200 that do. Worse, because the index on just `CustomerId` doesn't include `Status` or the other displayed columns, each of those 4,000 rows also needs a **Key Lookup** — a separate trip back into the clustered index to fetch the rest of the row's data — before the residual filter can even be checked. So you end up doing 4,000 seeks-plus-lookups purely to arrive at 200 rows you actually wanted.

Why is this such a sneaky trap, more so than a plain missing-index scenario? Because a Scan is an obvious, visually loud red flag — everyone learns to be suspicious of a big Table Scan or Clustered Index Scan. A residual predicate, by contrast, hides *inside* what looks like a perfectly normal, healthy-looking Index Seek. You have to actually expand the seek operator's properties in the plan and look specifically at the **Seek Predicate** property versus the separate **Predicate** property to notice that only part of your filter made it into the efficient seek, and the rest is being quietly checked afterward, row by row, on data that already required an expensive trip to fetch. Someone who only glances at the operator icons — 'ah, an Index Seek, good, moving on' — will walk right past this, exactly the same way someone glancing at a multi-join plan can walk past one bad join buried deeper in the tree. The other telltale sign, even without digging into seek-predicate details, is a mismatch between logical reads and the final row count: if a query returns 200 rows but the plan shows reads and lookups proportional to 4,000, that gap is the residual predicate's fingerprint.

The fix is conceptually simple: don't just index the column you filter on *some* of the time — index the *combination* of columns you actually filter on together, in the right order, so all of them become part of the seek predicate instead of leaving some as residual afterthoughts. A composite index built as `(CustomerId, Status)` changes everything: now both `CustomerId = 42` and `Status = 'Open'` can be used together to seek directly to exactly the ~200 matching rows — no residual filtering needed, because the entire WHERE clause is now expressible as a seek predicate against the index's key. Adding the displayed column (`Total`) as an `INCLUDE` on top of that makes the index fully covering too, eliminating the Key Lookups as well. The rewritten query seeks straight to ~200 rows and is done — no wasted work fetching and then discarding the other 3,800.

The broader habit to take away from this lesson: whenever you're checking whether an index is really doing its job, don't stop at 'is this a Seek or a Scan' — look one level deeper, at the Seek Predicate versus any residual Predicate, and compare the number of rows actually read against the number of rows the query finally returns. A big gap between those two numbers, even under a seek, means part of your filter isn't being used to narrow the search at all — it's just cleaning up after the fact.

## Scenario
Finding one customer's `Open` orders uses the index on `CustomerId` — the plan even shows an Index Seek. Yet it does far more work than the small result suggests. The index only gets you *part* of the way.

## Why it's slow
`IX_Orders_CustomerId` covers only `CustomerId`, so the **seek predicate** is `CustomerId = 42` — and that matches all **4,000** of that customer's orders. `Status = 'Open'` isn't in the index, so it can only be applied as a **residual predicate** *after* the engine looks each of those 4,000 rows up in the clustered index. You seek to 4,000 rows and a key-lookup on every one, just to keep the ~200 that are Open.

## What to look for
- An Index Seek whose **Seek Predicate** is only `CustomerId`, with `Status` shown as a **Predicate** (residual), plus a Key Lookup / Nested Loops.
- Reads far larger than the final row count — the tell-tale of a residual filter.

## The concept
Put the columns you filter on **into the index key** so they become seek predicates, not residuals. A composite index `(CustomerId, Status)` (INCLUDE `Total`) seeks directly to `CustomerId = 42 AND Status = 'Open'` — ~200 rows, covered, no lookups. The difference between a *seek predicate* and a *residual predicate* is the difference between reading 200 rows and reading 4,000.
hints: The seek only uses CustomerId; Status is a residual predicate applied after looking up all 4,000 of the customer's orders.
Move Status into the index key so it becomes part of the seek, and cover Total to avoid the lookups.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Cust_Status ON Orders(CustomerId, Status) INCLUDE (Total); then re-run.
